result.reading: Blocks 15–16 present the royal grant and its gold card as pure largesse. This paragraph springs the trap: it lets slip that everything the card pays for is a single debt that keeps swelling, and that staying at the Academy only suspends the interest, perhaps for life. The closing maxim then explains why the grant was never a gift. It answers block 14 (why Theodore can no longer afford to leave), is picked up at once by block 18, which calls staying on the real difficulty and sets the opposite fate against this deferral (leave after the fourth circle and the debt can never be repaid), and blocks 19–20 show the work that awaits those who drop out.

elements.source: можна було навіть ніколи не платити відсотків
elements.where: where the narrator says what staying at the Academy means for paying interest on the debt
elements.what: Staying brings an exemption, not a hardship: it suspends the duty to pay interest. The time word makes that suspension potentially permanent, which is literal for the residents who stay on to grey hair and the grave (block 2). The degree word ranks this as the furthest perk yet, capping a list that has just climbed to designer clothes and houses (block 16, which also tops its list with a degree word). That is the irony: this 'best' perk is exactly what lets the debt swell. In a fast English rendering the degree word tends to slide behind the negative, which turns permission into inability (one would be too poor to pay even the interest). That collapses the two sides of the trap, because block 18 sets the opposite fate against this one: whoever leaves after the fourth circle can never repay.

checks.ask: Does the translation say that staying lets one skip paying the interest (one is allowed or able not to pay it), rather than that one is unable to pay it?
checks.fail: The sentence says, or most naturally reads, that one cannot pay or afford even the interest, or that the interest has to be paid.

checks.ask: Is not paying interest marked as a surprising extreme, going further than one would expect, rather than stated as a plain fact or a mere addition?
checks.fail: No word or turn marks the surpassing degree. The exemption is stated flatly or simply added to the list.

checks.ask: Does the translation say that one might never pay the interest, at no time at all, rather than only that one need not pay it?
checks.fail: The time scope is missing: the text only says one need not or did not have to pay, or limits the exemption to some period.

elements.source: І якщо залишатися в Академії, можна було навіть ніколи не платити відсотків за боргом, що нескінченно зростав.
elements.where: the sentence about staying at the Academy, paying interest, and the growing debt
elements.what: The sentence states a rule of the system for anyone who stays. The original builds it from three parts: a condition in the infinitive with no subject, an impersonal past-tense modal of possibility, and a degree word placed in front of a negated adverb of time. A past-tense relative clause closes it. English has none of these shapes, so a close rendering comes out with no proper subject, an impersonal frame, a degree word stranded before a negative, or tenses that drift within the sentence.

checks.ask: At this spot, does the translation read as written by a skilled native writer?
checks.fail: It reads as translated, for example: a degree word placed directly before a negative ('could even never pay'); an impersonal 'it was possible to...'; a dangling 'if staying...' clause with no subject; or a present-tense condition clashing with past-tense narration in the same sentence.

elements.where: where the debt itself first appears, together with its growth
elements.what: Blocks 15–16 present the royal grant and its gold card as pure largesse. Here the narrator mentions in passing, as if the reader had known all along, that all of it is a single debt, unbounded in its growth. The reader realises the grant was a loan from the start, and that the perk of skipping interest is exactly what makes it swell. The effect rests on three parts: the debt is recognisably the card's own, it goes on growing, and the narrator does not point at the twist.

checks.ask: Can the reader tell that this is the debt already in play, the one the card's spending runs up, rather than some new, unspecified debt?
checks.fail: The debt is brought in as a new, indefinite or generic debt. Nothing ties it to the card: no definite or possessive reference and no mention of the card.

checks.ask: Is the debt said to keep on growing (an ongoing increase that does not stop), rather than merely being large, endless, or already grown?
checks.fail: The debt is only large, endless or grown, or its growth carries no sense of continuing.

checks.ask: Is the twist left for the reader to infer, with no added words announcing that the grant or card was really a loan, and nothing calling the arrangement a trap or a catch?
checks.fail: The translation adds such an announcement or comment.

elements.where: the closing general statement about what one could get in Seraph
elements.what: This is a familiar everyday saying, turned on Seraph. It denies that anything there is gratuitous: every benefit entails payment. That is its job here; it explains, after the fact, why the generous-sounding grant turned out to be a debt. Taken word by word, the idiom becomes a remark about manner or suddenness. It can also be misread as being about reasons or chance, or about things coming easily. Each of these drops the payment, and with it the link to the debt.

checks.ask: Does the closing line say that nothing in Seraph came without a price, that nothing was given as a gift?
checks.fail: The line instead speaks of manner or suddenness (a word-for-word rendering of the idiom), of reasons or chance, or of ease and effort, so no price or obligation in return is implied.

elements.where: the closing general statement about Seraph: how it is tied to the sentence before it, and how sweeping its denial is
elements.what: The closing line is offered as the reason for what precedes. This follows the narrator's habit of explaining with a causal opener (blocks 3, 5, 6): the debt follows from how Seraph works. The denial is also absolute, pressed home by an intensifier: a bitter, sweeping hyperbole in the narrator's usual manner (block 16 stresses the living costs with the same intensifier). A hurried rendering often drops the connector, leaving a free-floating maxim, or trims the intensifier, leaving a milder general remark.

checks.ask: Is the closing line presented as the reason for or explanation of the debt, rather than as an unconnected remark or a contrast?
checks.fail: No word or turn makes it a reason (it simply follows as a separate statement), or it is linked by a contrast or concession.

checks.ask: Is the denial reinforced by an intensifier, so that the rule reads as absolute and emphatic?
checks.fail: The denial is bare and unreinforced, or softened to most things or almost nothing.
